content.text: Ramakrishna was born in the village of Kamarpukar, in the Zillah Hugli, on the 20th of February, 1833. His father, Khudiram Chattopadhyaya, was the head of the only Brahmanic family in the village and, though very poor, 'would rather starve than stray from the strictest path of Brahmanical orthodoxy.' The name given to the child was Gadadhara, a name of Vishnu, given on account of a dream in which the deity told his father he would be born as his son; it was only later in life that he began to be called Ramakrishna.
content.source_name: Ramakrishna, His Life and Sayings, by F. Max Muller, 'Ramakrishna's Life' (London: Longmans, Green, and Co., 1898)

content.text: When his elder brother fell ill, Ramakrishna took charge of worship at the temple of the goddess Kali at Dakshineswar, and 'began to look upon the image of the goddess Kali as his mother and the mother of the universe. He believed it to be living and breathing and taking food out of his hand.' After the regular forms of worship he would sit for hours, singing hymns and praying to her as a child to his mother, 'till he lost all consciousness of the outward world.'
content.source_name: Ramakrishna, His Life and Sayings, by F. Max Muller, 'Ramakrishna's Life' (London: Longmans, Green, and Co., 1898)

content.text: Ramakrishna underwent 'twelve years of unheard-of tapasya, or ascetic exercises,' during which, he later recalled, 'a great religious tornado, as it were, raged within him.' He never once slept soundly through those years; he wept for hours calling out, 'Mother, oh my mother, another day has gone, and still I have not found thee,' and prayed, 'Mother! destroy in me all idea that I am great, and that I am a Brahman, and that they are low and pariahs, for who are they but Thou in so many forms?'
content.source_name: Ramakrishna, His Life and Sayings, by F. Max Muller, 'Ramakrishna's Life' (London: Longmans, Green, and Co., 1898)

content.text: To teach his own soul detachment from wealth, Ramakrishna would sit by the Ganges with gold and silver coins in one hand and a handful of rubbish in the other, telling himself, 'this is what the world calls money... but it can never help thee to realise the ever-existent knowledge and bliss, the Brahman. Regard it, therefore, as rubbish,' before throwing both into the river. When a wealthy disciple once draped him in a costly gold-fringed shawl, he threw it to the ground and used it to clean the floor, saying it 'increases vanity, but it can never help to realise the ever-existent knowledge and bliss, and therefore is no better than a piece of torn rag.'
content.source_name: Ramakrishna, His Life and Sayings, by F. Max Muller, 'Ramakrishna's Life' (London: Longmans, Green, and Co., 1898)

content.text: Of how seekers were drawn to him without his seeking fame, Ramakrishna himself observed: 'When the rose is blown, and sheds its fragrance all around, the bees come of themselves. The bees seek the full-blown rose, and not the rose the bees.' He came to teach that all religions are true, 'though each of them takes account of one aspect only' of the one undivided and eternal reality -- having in turn practiced Vaishnava devotion, Vedantic renunciation, and even, in his later years, Christian and Islamic contemplation, each time arriving quickly at what he held to be their common core.
content.source_name: Ramakrishna, His Life and Sayings, by F. Max Muller, 'Ramakrishna's Life' (London: Longmans, Green, and Co., 1898)

content.text: In his final illness, from what began as 'the clergyman's throat' and developed into cancer, physicians advised Ramakrishna to keep strict silence, but he would not. Crowds gathered wherever he went and waited to hear a word from him, and 'he, out of compassion for them, would not remain silent,' saying, 'I would suffer willingly all sorts of bodily pains, and death also, a hundred thousand times, if by so doing I could bring one single soul to freedom and salvation.' He died on the night of 16 August 1886, passing into a samadhi from which, unlike his daily trances, he did not return.
content.source_name: Ramakrishna, His Life and Sayings, by F. Max Muller, 'Ramakrishna's Life' (London: Longmans, Green, and Co., 1898)

content.text: Ramakrishna felt such aversion to gold and silver that he could not touch them without physical distress, and he twice declined offers of a temple and a substantial yearly income, saying he would have to flee the place if the gift were pressed on him. Of himself he would say only that he was 'servant of all men and women,' looking on them all as God, and would touch the ground reverently where his own disciples had walked -- a humility his followers, including the young Narendranath Datta who became Swami Vivekananda, carried forward as the foundation of his teaching.
content.source_name: Ramakrishna, His Life and Sayings, by F. Max Muller, 'Ramakrishna's Life' (London: Longmans, Green, and Co., 1898)
